chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: Radio air time and early records for Bluebird and Brunswick labels
summary: He recalls broadcasts, six to eight Bluebird sides recorded in a New Orleans loft, and cheap Brunswick cover-label dates where an executive rejected a Benny Carter arrangement.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: You broadcast from there, didn't you?

Yes. We had a lot of air time. That was the whole idea. Sitting there with no money, was to get the air time. We were recording. We had made some records prior to that. We made some records in New Orleans for Bluebird. Eli Oberstein came through town with the portable unit and we recorded in some loft up there and we made six sides there, six or eight, I forget how many. Not any more than eight.
I think they're in here, right?
They tell that story about recording circumstances, in those liner notes.

And then I had done some dates with -- up at Brunswick for some of those there, cover labels like Perfect and Mellotone, and the kind of dates where you just walk in and meet and carve up a stock orchestration or something and play it. In fact they had Benny Carter make some arrangements for some of those things, and oh, Joe Higgins was in charge of it. He just hit the ceiling. He

said, 'What are you trying to do to me?' 'All this doodley doop.' He said, 'We just want the melody.' And he cut -- in fact one of Benny Carter's arrangements, he just said, 'That, I won't even issue that.' And it was great, you know. And we had to come back and make the stock orchestration of the tune later, about a week later or something like that.
